Five minutes. The agent reviews the eval loop's run and sharpens the generator's tactic file one more time. ## People absorb what they already half know

People take up what they already half know. That is not a statement about willingness. It is the plain shape of how anyone absorbs anything: you recognise the new thing by what it resembles in the work you already do, and if it resembles nothing, you have nowhere to put it.

Michael Polanyi, a philosopher of science, had the line for it: *we know more than we can tell.* Your agent runs on the part of your work you could never have written down. The teammate you are handing it to has their own version of that, about their own work, and it is the only place your thing can land.

You felt this an hour ago. Like most teams, you filled the technical plan quickly. The people plan stalled on names.

That was not the exercise being hard. That was the exercise being accurate. A missing name is a finding: it marks the part of this that is not built yet, and it is the part that decides whether any of the rest gets used.

So the move stays small. One name. One person whose week this would change, who would tell you plainly if it did not.

## Pick against the outcome

The agent then compares candidates from `patterns/personal-to-team-patterns.md` against that outcome and writes your choice to `module-7/branch.md`.

The four sharing strategies are:

1. **Share the context.** Your `memory/`, `sources/`, root instructions, and `style.md` travel. Teammates build on top.
2. **Share a skill.** Extract one scoped capability. Teammates plug it in, unlike the usual shelfware.
3. **Share the output (push).** Schedule the agent. Output lands where the team looks.
4. **Share an interface (pull).** Wrap the agent. Teammates invoke it through a bot, mention, form, or endpoint.

*"Share the whole agent"* is a vendor pitch and is NOT on the list.

Read `module-7/branch.md`. Every picked candidate should name how it moves the teammate's outcome; infrastructure should appear only as a constraint. If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.

## The judge names its own limit

The winner (or an ensemble of the top two) becomes a judge file you carry forward.

Not certainty. Certainty isn't available. What you buy is a *grounded choice about grounding*: you know which detector won on your material, you know why, you know what it misses, and the judge file you save plainly names its own blind spot.

That last clause is the one that matters. Grounded output names what it doesn't know. A grounded judge names what it can't catch. Ungrounded output pretends to know everything; a cargo-cult judge pretends to catch everything. The difference looks small on the page. In a decision room, it's the difference between a memo that holds up and a memo that detonates.
